author: Anonymous
occasion: The work preserves a sequential record of Bishop Cyprian's interrogations, condemnation, and execution at Carthage for communal memory. It does not state its purpose directly beyond the closing doxology.
argument: Before Paternus at Carthage, Cyprian confesses he is a Christian and bishop who worships only the one true creator God and refuses to perform Roman rites, and he evades naming the presbyters by citing laws against informers and saying they can be found in their own cities. Exiled to Curubis, he is later recalled and brought before Galerius Maximus, where he again admits his identity and leadership and flatly refuses to perform the imperially ordered rites. Galerius Maximus, after consulting his council, condemns him as an organizer of an unlawful association hostile to Roman gods and laws. Cyprian is executed by the sword, thanks God for the sentence, and is honorably carried away by Christians by night for burial.

outline.move: Paternus interrogates Cyprian at Carthage about his religion, hears his confession, orders exile to Curubis, asks for the presbyters, and relays the emperors' order that no assemblies be held and cemeteries not be entered on pain of death.

After Galerius Maximus succeeds Paternus, Cyprian, staying in his gardens by sacred command and expecting to be fetched, is taken by two officers to Sexti, lodged overnight, and brought before Galerius Maximus, where he again confesses and refuses to perform the rites.
Galerius Maximus consults his council and pronounces sentence of execution by the sword, which Cyprian receives with thanks to God.

Cyprian is led to the field at Sexti, prays, removes his outer garments and hands his dalmatic to deacons, orders his attendants to give twenty-five gold coins to the executioner, has linen cloths laid before him by the brothers, is blindfolded with help, is executed by the sword, and his body is later carried away by night for burial.
The narrator gives the date of the martyrdom under Valerian and Gallienus and closes with a doxology to Christ.

scripture: The only biblical language is Cyprian's creator formula in section 1, qui fecit caelum et terram, mare et quae sunt in eis omnia, alluding to Exodus 20:11, Acts 4:24, Acts 14:15, and Revelation 10:6. No book is formally quoted and no book titles or Psalms occur, so no LXX/Vulgate naming or Psalm-numbering conventions can be established from this text.
uncertain: Composition date and place beyond shortly after the 258 events are not established from the text.
Catalogue calls this an early Christian Greek work, but the supplied source text is Latin.
Exact modern equivalents and locations for Curubitana, Sexti, Saturni, Venerea, Salutaria, Sauciolum, Macrobian grounds, Mappalian Way, and pools are not established from the text.
Two words are garbled in transmission, including a staff rank in section 3 and a numeral or word in section 4, so duties and details there cannot be fixed.
Whether Paternus and the ablative Aspasio Paterno are one person with full name Aspasius Paternus cannot be established from wording alone.
No scriptural citation conventions can be established because the text contains only an unmarked creator-formula allusion.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Cyprian evades naming the presbyters by citing laws against informers and saying they can be found in their own cities
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Cyprianus episcopus respondit: Legibus vestris bene atque utiliter censuistis delatores non esse. itaque detegi et deferri a me non possunt. in civitatibus autem suis invenientur.
_unresolved_facts.fix: Cyprian evades naming the presbyters by citing that the laws have rightly and usefully decreed that there should be no informers (delatores), so they cannot be revealed and denounced by him; he says they will be found in their own cities, not that they can be found there by Paternus

_unresolved_facts.claim: Cyprian is executed by the sword, thanks God for the sentence
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Thascium Cyprianum gladio animadverti placet. Cyprianus episcopus dixit: Deo gratias.
_unresolved_facts.fix: Cyprian thanks God upon hearing the sentence of execution by the sword, not after the execution itself

_unresolved_facts.claim: Paternus interrogates Cyprian at Carthage about his religion, hears his confession, orders exile to Curubis, asks for the presbyters, and relays the emperors' order that no assemblies be held and cemeteries not be entered on pain of death
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Paternus proconsul dixit: Poteris ergo secundum praeceptum Valeriani et Gallieni exsul ad urbem Curubitanam proficisci? Cyprianus episcopus dixit: Proficiscor.
_unresolved_facts.fix: Paternus asks if Cyprian can go into exile to Curubis; Cyprian agrees to go (Proficiscor). The exile is not unilaterally 'ordered' as a command—Paternus frames it as a question about ability and Cyprian consents

_unresolved_facts.claim: Cyprian, staying in his gardens by sacred command
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ex sacro praecepto in suis hortis manebat
_unresolved_facts.fix: Cyprian stays in his gardens 'by sacred command' (ex sacro praecepto)—the brief should clarify this refers to divine/sacred command, not an imperial command

The text states Cyprian 'suffered' (passus est) and was prepared for execution, but does not explicitly narrate the moment of execution by the sword; the executioner's arrival and payment are mentioned, then the text moves to burial

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: successit Aspasio Paterno proconsuli Galerius Maximus proconsul
_unresolved_facts.fix: Aspasius Paternus (nominative would be Aspasius Paternus; the ablative Aspasio Paterno is the form in the text, but the brief should list the nominative form for consistency with other entries)

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: turba fratrum dicebat: Et nos cum ipso decollemur
_unresolved_facts.fix: turba fratrum dicebat in section 6, but the brief should note this is a crowd exclamation, not a formal speech; also the content 'Et nos cum ipso decollemur' is a request to be beheaded with him, not a sustained voice

_unresolved_facts.claim: Cyprian is honorably carried away by Christians by night for burial
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: eiusque corpus propter gentilium curiositatem in proximo positum est. inde per noctem sublatum cum cereis et scolacibus ad areas Macrobii Candidiani procuratoris...deductum est
_unresolved_facts.fix: Cyprian's body is first placed nearby because of Gentile curiosity, then taken away by night with candles and torches to the grounds of Macrobius Candidianus; the text does not specify 'by Christians' though this is implied
